title: Going home well: changing how our ward discharges patients
question: How should our ward change the way it sends patients home, so fewer come back within 30 days?
summary: A worked example about how a hospital ward organises its work. It is not medical advice, and every name, quote and number is invented. A 28-bed medical ward sees one in seven patients readmitted within a month, often because of confusion about medicines. This map follows a patient's way home and the ward's discharge day, and lists what the team needs to decide.

reading: This is a worked example about how a ward organises its work; it is not medical advice and everything in it is invented. The first view follows a patient and their carer home: how it goes today, how it would go with the proposed changes, and what the carer goes through. The second view shows the ward's side: the evening list, getting medicines ready, discharge day itself, and the calls and letters afterwards. Each box says whether it works today, partly works, is missing, or is planned. Turn on Show technical names to see which systems, forms and roles are involved. Notes from the pharmacist, ward manager, quality analyst, patient voice and others sit on the boxes they are about.

checked.note: Checked against a six-month ward audit, patient and carer feedback, a staff huddle, two weeks of timing observations, calls with five family doctor practices, a language and access sample, and a two-week try-out of follow-up calls. All invented.

glossary.discharge: When a patient leaves hospital to go home or to another place of care.
glossary.readmission: Coming back into hospital within a set time after leaving, here 30 days.
glossary.discharge letter: The summary sent to the patient's family doctor about their stay and their medicines.
glossary.tomorrow's list: The patients the team expects to send home the next day, agreed the evening before.
glossary.ward round: When the doctors see each patient on the ward, usually in the morning, and decide the plan for the day.
glossary.discharge lounge: A room where patients who are ready to go can wait for transport or medicines, freeing their bed.
glossary.handover: When one shift tells the next about every patient.
glossary.say back: Asking the patient to explain in their own words, to check they understood.

evidence.text: 58 of 412 patients (14%) were readmitted within 30 days.
In 21 of those 58, the notes record a problem with medicines at home.
63% of discharges happen after 4 pm. The pharmacy closes at 5:30 pm.
Discharge letters reached the family doctor within 24 hours for 71% of patients.
Everyone was kind, but I left with a bag of tablets and no idea which were new.
We were told he'd go home in the morning. We waited until 7 pm for his medicines.
Nobody rang me afterwards. I didn't know who to call when I felt worse.
A simple sheet saying what changed would have helped more than anything.
If we knew the night before, we could have medicines ready by noon.
The discharge checklist is on paper and often half-filled when the patient leaves.
Follow-up phone calls happen when there is time, which is rarely.
Average time from 'can go home' to medicines on the ward: 5 hours 40 minutes.
Discharge medicines reach the pharmacy queue in a batch, mostly between 12 pm and 2 pm.
Hospital transport must be booked by 11 am for a same-day journey; 1 in 5 patients needs it.
The discharge lounge had free chairs before noon and was full after 3 pm on 9 of 10 days.
Weekend discharges are about half of a weekday's, partly because no pharmacist is on the ward.
Four of five practices said the most useful part of the letter is what changed with medicines and why.
Three of five practices said letters sometimes arrive after the patient has already phoned them.
Two practices asked for one named contact on the ward for questions in the first week.
About 8% of patients need an interpreter; telephone interpreting takes 20 to 40 minutes to connect.
Discharge papers are printed in English only, in small type.
About 1 in 4 patients go home to live alone.
Large print and a picture of each tablet would help my mum.
Of 31 patients called within two days, 28 were reached; 9 had a question about medicines.
Average call: 7 minutes; afternoon calls were answered more often.
I could only do this because two planned meetings were cancelled.
Discharges bunch up after the afternoon ward round.

gaps.title: Tomorrow's list, agreed the evening before
gaps.why: Lets the pharmacy get medicines ready by noon instead of the evening.

stories.as: As the ward pharmacist, I want tomorrow's list by 6 pm, so medicines are ready by noon.
done_when: a list is agreed at the evening handover every weekday
at least 70% of listed patients leave before 2 pm
the list never sends anyone home before a doctor confirms in the morning

stories.as: As a carer, I want to know the evening before roughly when to come, so I do not lose a day waiting.
done_when: carers of listed patients are told a likely time the evening before
they are called if the plan changes on the morning round

gaps.title: A one-page 'what changed' sheet
gaps.why: Medicine confusion is behind about a third of readmissions on this ward.

stories.as: As a patient going home, I want one page showing new, changed and stopped medicines, so I take the right ones.
done_when: every discharge includes the sheet
the nurse goes through it with the patient or carer
patients can say back which medicines are new

stories.as: As a patient with poor eyesight, I want the sheet in large print, so I can read it at home.
done_when: the sheet uses large type by default
it fits on one page

stories.as: As a patient who needs an interpreter, I want the sheet explained in my language, so I understand it.
done_when: an interpreter is booked the evening before for listed patients who need one
the say-back is done with the interpreter

gaps.title: A call within two days
gaps.why: Patients did not know who to call when they felt worse; in the try-out 9 of 28 had a medicine question.

stories.as: As a patient at home, I want a call within two days, so I can ask questions before small problems grow.
done_when: 90% of patients get a call within two working days
the call follows a short script and is recorded

stories.as: As the discharge coordinator, I want protected time for calls, so they do not depend on cancelled meetings.
done_when: two hours each weekday afternoon are kept for calls
the ward manager reviews call numbers weekly

stories.as: As a nurse, I want the checklist in the ward system, so nothing is missed and the next shift can see it.
done_when: a patient cannot be marked discharged with required items blank

stories.as: As the next shift's nurse, I want to see what is done and what is not, so nothing is repeated or missed.
done_when: the checklist shows who did each item and when
say-back and 'sheet given' are required items

gaps.title: Letters the family doctor can act on
gaps.why: Practices said the medicines part is what matters, and letters sometimes arrive after the patient phones.

stories.as: As a family doctor, I want what changed with medicines at the top of the letter, so I can act quickly.
done_when: every letter starts with new, changed and stopped medicines

stories.as: As a practice, I want one named contact on the ward for the first week, so I can ask questions.

notes.title: Patients asked for a simple sheet
notes.body: Carers said one page of what changed would help more than anything.
notes.recommend: Write the sheet with two patients and two carers before the trial.
notes.question: Who from our patient group can help write and test the sheet?

notes.title: Noon is possible with a night-before list
notes.body: The pharmacist said medicines could be ready by noon if they knew the evening before.
notes.recommend: Start with weekdays only; weekends have one pharmacist.
notes.question: Can we run tomorrow's list on weekdays first and add weekends later?

notes.title: The list must not rush anyone out
notes.body: A list made the evening before could pressure staff to discharge patients who are not ready.
notes.recommend: Being on the list means 'medicines prepared', never 'must leave'. A doctor confirms each morning.
notes.question: How do we make clear that the list is a plan, not a promise?

notes.title: Measure the right readmissions
notes.body: Some readmissions have nothing to do with discharge. Counting all of them could hide the effect.
notes.recommend: Track readmissions linked to medicines separately, as well as the total.
notes.question: Which readmissions count as 'linked to medicines', and who decides?

notes.title: Watch for side effects of the change
notes.body: Calling every patient takes coordinator time from somewhere else.
notes.recommend: Record what the calls find and how long they take.
notes.question: What would we stop doing to make time for the calls?

notes.title: One number, staffed when people need it
notes.body: A number nobody answers is worse than none.
notes.recommend: Use the ward's existing advice line and say on the sheet when it is answered.
notes.question: Can the advice line cope with more calls in the evenings?

notes.title: Try it for eight weeks, then decide
notes.body: Small changes, tested quickly, are easier to keep or drop.
notes.recommend: Run all three changes for eight weeks and review at a team meeting.
notes.question: Do we start all three changes together, or one at a time?

notes.title: Calls must reach the right person
notes.body: Calling a home number could reach someone the patient did not want told.
notes.recommend: Ask each patient at discharge which number to call and who may answer.
notes.question: Where do we record the patient's call preferences?

notes.title: An assistant could draft the sheet
notes.body: The changes are already in the medicines record; drafting the sheet is routine.
notes.recommend: An assistant drafts the sheet from the record; the pharmacist checks and signs it before the patient sees it.
notes.question: Are we comfortable with a drafted sheet if a pharmacist always checks it?

notes.title: Calls cost time; readmissions cost more
notes.body: Each readmission uses a bed for several days. A short call takes about ten minutes.
notes.recommend: Count coordinator hours during the trial to compare.
notes.question: Can we fund extra coordinator hours for eight weeks?

notes.title: The batch after the round is the real delay
notes.body: Prescriptions arrive in one batch between 12 and 2 pm, so nothing can be ready early.
notes.recommend: Work from tomorrow's list overnight, and leave the post-round batch for surprises only.
notes.question: Can the pharmacy staff an early-morning slot for listed patients?

notes.title: A pharmacist always checks the sheet
notes.body: A wrong sheet is worse than no sheet.
notes.recommend: No sheet is printed without a pharmacist's check.
notes.question: Who checks sheets when the ward pharmacist is off?

notes.title: Weekends need a pharmacist
notes.body: Without one, weekend discharges stay at half a weekday's.
notes.recommend: Try a Saturday-morning pharmacist during the eight weeks.
notes.question: Can we fund a Saturday pharmacist for the trial?

notes.title: Use the lounge in the morning
notes.body: The lounge is empty before noon and full after 3 pm.
notes.recommend: Move listed patients to the lounge once medicines are ready.
notes.question: Who decides when a patient moves to the lounge?

notes.title: Calls need protected time
notes.body: The try-out only worked because meetings were cancelled.
notes.recommend: Protect two hours each weekday afternoon for calls during the trial.
notes.question: What do we stop doing to free those two hours?

notes.title: Leave weekends until the weekday version works
notes.body: Weekends add staffing questions.
notes.recommend: Start weekdays only; review weekends at week four.
notes.question: Do we agree to start weekdays only?

notes.title: Say-back gives us something to measure
notes.body: We cannot measure understanding from a ticked 'sheet given' box.
notes.recommend: Record whether the patient could say back the new medicines.
notes.question: Is a yes/no for say-back enough, or do we need more detail?

notes.title: Check the list does not change who goes home
notes.body: The list must change timing, not decisions.
notes.recommend: Compare who goes home and when, before and during the trial.
notes.question: What would tell us the list is pushing people out too early?

notes.title: Letters on the same day for listed patients
notes.body: Today 71% reach the practice within 24 hours.
notes.recommend: Measure same-day letters separately for listed patients.
notes.question: Do we aim for same-day letters for everyone, or listed patients first?

notes.title: Large print and pictures
notes.body: A patient group member asked for large print and a picture of each tablet.
notes.recommend: Test a large-print sheet with three patients before the trial.
notes.question: Do we add pictures of tablets, or is that too hard to keep right?

notes.title: The carer will be the one sorting tablets
notes.body: Carers are often shown the medicines quickly, if at all.
notes.recommend: Go through the sheet with the carer present or on speakerphone.
notes.question: What do we do when the carer cannot be there?

notes.title: Calls must be recorded in the ward record
notes.body: Notes kept elsewhere would not be seen by the next person.
notes.recommend: Use a short call form in the ward record; no personal notebooks.
notes.question: Who can see call records after the patient leaves?

notes.title: Use professional interpreters, not family
notes.body: Family members interpreting can miss or change things about medicines.
notes.recommend: Book telephone interpreters the evening before for listed patients.
notes.question: Do we allow family to interpret if an interpreter cannot be reached?

notes.title: Old medicines at home cause mix-ups
notes.body: The audit found old medicines still being taken.
notes.recommend: Say on the sheet which medicines to stop, and offer to take back old ones.
notes.question: Can the ward take back old medicines from home?

notes.title: One in four go home to live alone
notes.body: For them there is no carer to ask.
notes.recommend: Call people living alone first.
notes.question: Do we call people living alone on day one rather than day two?

notes.title: A time, not just a day
notes.body: Carers took a day off and waited hours.
notes.recommend: Give carers a likely time the evening before.
notes.question: How do we tell carers if the time changes?

notes.title: An assistant could draft the sheet from the medicines list
notes.body: Comparing before and after lists and writing plain reasons is routine.
notes.recommend: Let an assistant draft; a pharmacist always checks and signs.
notes.question: Do we let an assistant draft the plain-language reason for each change?

notes.title: An assistant could prepare the call list
notes.body: Yesterday's discharges, who lives alone, and preferred times are all in the record.
notes.recommend: Prepare the list by 1 pm, people living alone first.
notes.question: Do we let an assistant put people in call order?

notes.title: Seven minutes a call
notes.body: About 30 calls a fortnight at 7 minutes is under four hours.
notes.recommend: Fund two coordinator hours a day for eight weeks.
notes.question: Is the call time worth it if readmissions fall by only a few?

notes.title: Booking transport earlier saves bed time
notes.body: Transport booked after 11 am means waiting until the next day.
notes.recommend: Book transport from tomorrow's list at 9 am.
notes.question: Do we measure bed hours saved, as well as readmissions?

notes.title: Tell patients the list is a plan
notes.body: Being told 'tomorrow' and then not going is upsetting and can push staff to rush.
notes.recommend: Use the words 'likely tomorrow, if the doctors agree in the morning'.
notes.question: Who says it, and in what words?

notes.title: One number that is answered
notes.body: Patients did not know who to call.
notes.recommend: Put one ward number on the sheet, answered until 8 pm.
notes.question: Can the ward answer that number until 8 pm?

decisions.question: Do we run an eight-week trial of tomorrow's list, the 'what changed' sheet and follow-up calls?
options: Sheet and list first, calls later

decisions.question: What do we measure, and what result would make us keep the changes?
Do we start on weekdays only?
options: Weekdays plus Saturday with a pharmacist

decisions.question: Who drafts and who checks the 'what changed' sheet?

outcomes.measure: Readmissions within 30 days linked to medicines

outcomes.target: 7 in 10 of those on tomorrow's list

outcomes.measure: Hours from 'can go home' to medicines on the ward
Patients who could say back their new medicines
